articles.blurb: In 1819, a future king saw Pompeii’s erotic art and blushed. It stayed hidden for the next two centuries
articles.description: The preserved ruins of Pompeii and Herculaneum, entombed for millennia by the disastrous eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, have, since excavations began in the mid-eighteenth century, been a gol…
paragraphs: The preserved ruins of Pompeii and Herculaneum, entombed for millennia by the disastrous eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, have, since excavations began in the mid-eighteenth century, been a goldmine of detail depicting day-to-day life in the Roman empire. A little too much detail, in fact. In 1819, when Francis I, heir to the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, visited the newly unearthed artifacts at what is now the National Archaeological Museum in Naples, hoping to marvel at the frescoes, paintings and sculptures that had been hidden for nearly two thousand years, he was so mortified by the explicit nature of the Roman art that he promptly ordered much of it to be hidden away again.

The future monarch’s acute embarrassment marked the inception of the Neapolitan museum’s Gabinetto Segreto—“secret room”—which would go on to hide a myriad of artworks depicting every conceivable act of lovemaking between women, men, gender-ambiguous figures and even gods (not to mention swans and goats). This evidence of the ancient Romans’ uninhibited attitude to sexual fantasy, pleasure and diversity was so at odds with the prudish Christian mores that had come to dominate Europe millennia later, the powers that be decided the public was better off shielded from it, lest they be corrupted.
The story of Pompeii…reveals how pornography has long been the battleground on which morality and power and control are contested.

The erotic paintings and sculptures hidden in the Gabinetto Segreto would, for most of the following two centuries, remain accessible only to learned men carrying either permits detailing evidence of their high moral standing, or bribes. Fear of the defiling power of Roman fantasy ran so deep that the entrance to the room was, at one point, bricked up entirely. Apart from a brief window during the height of the sexual revolution, the “secret room” remained largely closed to the public until 2000. When it finally reopened, it was accompanied by educational texts, as the Gabinetto Segreto’s scientific curator Floriana Miele told me, that were meant to help visitors understand ancient Roman attitudes towards fertility, life and pleasure and prevent the works from being seen through our own era’s more crude perspective on the erotic.

After all, much of the art left behind by people in antiquity suggested that they had a “very different way of thinking about life and nature,” Miele said. But, as Christianity spread across Europe, attitudes began to shift. By the Middle Ages a distinct “attitude of prudish secrecy” had taken hold—a mindset that Miele said would prove particularly conducive to “prurient curiosity.” This is the mindset in which we remain stuck today, and it is partly responsible for the mess we’re now in. The story of Pompeii not only shows us how the definitions of the sexually acceptable and taboo have continued to change over time but reveals how pornography has long been the battleground on which morality and power and control are contested.

Perhaps precisely because it was forbidden, the erotic art of Pompeii and Herculaneum became highly influential to the Western understanding of pornography, even inspiring its first English-language dictionary definition. The word itself has ancient Greek roots—pornē, meaning prostitute, and graphien, meaning writing—and originally referred to texts or depictions related to sex work. But in 1864 Webster’s, an American dictionary, defined it as visual stimuli intended to elicit sexual desire—or, more specifically, “licentious painting […] examples of which exist in Pompeii.” Fueled by frenzied media interest in the Neapolitan excavations, the artifacts of Pompeii had effectively entered nineteenth-century pop culture. But choosing such an ancient reference to define pornography also allowed a kind of respectful distance and, perhaps, a feigned ignorance of the more contemporary erotic material in circulation at the time, from flagellation novels and clandestine memoirs to the explicit photographs and prints that were being passed discreetly across drawing rooms.
articles.title: A Technological History of Ancient Porn

articles.blurb: Kurt Gödel left behind thousands of pages of unpublished jottings about math and logic. Turns out he discovered much more than anyone realized
articles.description: Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems
paragraphs: The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.
After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.

Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.
The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.

“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”

Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.

In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.

Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team.

In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature.
“The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.”
articles.title: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths

articles.blurb: Truisms, abstractions, and flatness. The key to admiring John Berger’s poetry is admitting that he has a tin ear
articles.description: Poems, readings, poetry news and the entire 110-year archive of POETRY magazine.
paragraphs: Sometimes, seeming pained, he would press his hands into his forehead, as if trying to prevent the thoughts from evaporating through his brow. He was forcing them down the channel that runs out of his mouth. Nearly every time the writer John Berger was interviewed on camera, he did this, often more than once. As Geoff Dyer comments in an introduction to Berger’s selected essays, “we come close to witnessing thought as an act of almost physical labour.” Berger’s gesture says: not almost.

The story of Berger’s life, told most fully in Tom Overton’s recent biography John Berger: From Life (Verso, 2026), attests to constant effort. He was born a century ago in London and lived to the age of ninety. In that time, he learned to draw, paint, and write; he published regularly in The New Statesman, The Observer, and New Society; he scripted television programs and starred in them; he published essays, criticism, nonfiction books, and novels, including the Booker Prize-winning G. (1972); he was married four times and lived among the émigré bohemians of London, the cosmopolitans of Geneva, and the peasants of the Haute-Savoie in southeastern France; he herded animals and worked harvests; and “more than anything else,” Overton says, “[he] was a writer of letters.”

For someone who produced so much, what would it mean for thought to be an act of physical labor? Clearly, I mean more than an art that finds the mind’s construction in the face. As in Berger’s hands, so on his page: there is something very manual and material about the writing itself, never mind the fact that he did so much of it.

We might nevertheless appreciate the scarcity of his poetic output exactly as we appreciate the delicate crimson stigmas of the purple crocus flower; approximately 75,000 of these flowers are needed to yield one pound of dry saffron. For readers, Berger’s poetry is a similar sort of rare harvest, the byproduct of his prosaic labor, heralding its own high price. His poetry insists on its costliness (or its rarity, which is the same thing) in two ways. First, the lines are universally short (one or two metrical feet, typically), and tend to stomp and halt rather than flow:
Though each sentence is a semantic unit, the stuttering cadence introduced by the line breaks reveals a certain effort in deciding—or digging up, as it more often feels—the syntax itself.

Second, Berger’s poems often introduce a labor of de- and re-contextualization for the reader, likely because most of his published poetry first appeared in print as part of his prose works. Novels like Pig Earth (1979), about the peasant community in a French alpine village, are seeded with little poems relating to the characters’ lifeworld. A Seventh Man (1975), his photo-essay documenting migrant laborers with Jean Mohr, contains verse about executed prisoners. It is tempting to experience these insertions as interruptions. (Even this interpretation would seem generous. How often have you come across a poem suddenly inserted into a novel and thought: I’m glad this is here?!) But Berger’s oeuvre is one long refusal of generic constraints. Dyer, whose first book, Ways of Telling (1986), is a study of Berger, has stated elsewhere that “John Berger radically altered and enlarged my ideas of what a book could be.” Indeed, we can see in Dyer’s own works—which, despite lacking poetry, contain much in the way of unexpected media—the salutary effects of what academics would call interdisciplinarity trickling down.
articles.title: A Mere 140 Pages

articles.blurb: David Graeber was a brilliant, influential thinker. He was also largely wrong and had a surprisingly dark view of humanity
articles.description: In a critical reassessment of David Graeber’s intellectual legacy, Kemp challenges the anthropologist’s central conviction that human societies are shaped primarily by collective imagination and can therefore be transformed by…
paragraphs: The anthropologist David Graeber, who died in 2020 at the age of 59, was a renowned scholar, bestselling author, and committed activist. His books ranged from a history of debt and humanity to a treatise on why much of the job market is composed of useless “bullshit jobs.” He was a central figure behind the 2011 Occupy Wall Street movement and Global Justice Movement, the co-founder of the Anti-Capitalist Convergences organizations, and his legacy continues through the David Graeber Institute. He was perhaps the most influential anthropologist and anarchist of the past two decades, whose work continues to shape how progressives across the world think about history, the world, and how to build a better future.

Across dozens of books, essays, and articles is one central idea, summarized in his best-known quote from the final pages of Direct Action: An Ethnography (2009): “The ultimate, hidden truth of the world is that it is something that we make, and could just as easily make differently.” In the same chapter, Graeber contrasts two conceptions of political reality. There is the right-wing vision that the world is shaped mainly by violent physical forces, and the left-wing view that imagination is the stronger source of power. Graeber’s work was in many ways an attempt to prove that the second view is correct.

Underlying this central idea about the ultimate truth of the world are two arguments that reappear across his work. The first is that human social forms, whether they be brutal dictatorship or fierce egalitarianism, begin as acts of play and imagination. Even kings and dictators originally started largely as temporary acts of theater. The second is a result of the first: that changing the world is mainly a matter of changing our beliefs.

In Graeber’s view, patriarchy, slavery, capitalism, and even the very idea of gods and kings are all make-believe games that we got “stuck” in. It was a grand vision of not just politics, but also the cosmos. He even speculated that the movement of electrons could simply be subatomic particles playing.

Graeber was a brilliant, provocative thinker who is remembered fondly with good reason. He also disliked blind obedience and would have wanted others to question and interrogate his ideas. This piece will do so. Unfortunately, his grand vision of the ultimate, hidden truth of the world—that imagination is the key shaper of the world—is largely wrong, how he thought we should approach political organizing is a dead end, and his work has a surprisingly dark view of humanity.

One of Graeber’s most revealing books is one of his least known. On Kings (2017), a collection of essays written with his mentor Marshall Sahlins, suggests that human imagination is the answer to some of the most important questions of history: why did kings arise, around 5,000 years ago, and why do they persist to this day?

In their telling, the origin of kings lies not in weapons or agriculture, but in a primordial part of human thinking. They claim that humans have always lived under “terrifying despots” who may seem imaginary to us today, but were real and threatening to our early ancestors. As they put it, “insofar as there is a primordial political state, it is authoritarianism.” Physical kings draw their power mainly from ancient imagination, not swords.
articles.title: Dark Imagination

articles.blurb: Lydia Davis on stoicism: “a philosophy that could accommodate not only one’s fear of death but even one’s dread of the apocalypse”
articles.description: I’m not happy that humanity may disappear, and I’m not really comforted by the idea that other species may survive....
paragraphs: It is somewhat​ intimidating to write about a subject you are just beginning to explore – in this case, Stoicism. But I brought it on myself. I chose the subject of Stoic philosophy because I was newly engrossed in it and did not want to turn my mind to other matters. So this is my own doing. But please forgive any lacunae.

I was, early on, asked by a friend how I came to be interested in the Stoics. I wouldn’t tell her, except to say, ‘by chance’. I wanted to try to write the answer here, and if you tell someone something ahead of writing it, that may take away all your desire to write it. My interest was sparked by chance, but there were probably several reasons for my responding to that chance.

Before I explain, I would first like to describe my reaction to an essay in the LRB of 22 January 2026, not because it awakened my interest in the Stoic philosophers, but because reading it revealed to me the way two of my assumptions have changed over time, especially under the influence of my reading of the Stoics.

I was attracted by a review discussing two books, Everything Must Go: Why We Are Obsessed with the End of the World by Dorian Lynskey and Hopeful Pessimism by Mara van der Lugt. I am one of those who believe we are facing the end of the world – the end of the world as we know it right now, and the end of the world I knew in my early childhood in the 1950s, a world which at that time seemed to me, safely enclosed as I was in a peaceful college town, living on a quiet, leafy street of houses in a neighbourhood where I roamed freely, returning to a yellow house harbouring an intact family, with enough to eat, and unaware of my parents’ financial and political worries, an unchangeably safe world. (I mention this because it is so often what we grow up knowing that conditions our expectations of life.) I am not obsessed with the end of the world, but I now act within that framework, within the assumption that the world is sliding into catastrophe. As for ‘hopeful pessimism’, I’m afraid that pessimism generally outweighs my very conditional modicum of hope, though I respect those who are hopeful and hope they are right.

I found, as I read the essay, which opened intriguingly and relevantly by describing the plot of a Georges Perec novel, that I disagreed strongly at a couple of points with the perspective of its author, Geoff Mann, and, further, with his assumption that his readers would share his perspective. And this surprised me, because it revealed to me that my thinking had really, measurably, shifted from what I take to be some common assumptions.

Mann’s first assumption is revealed by his posing the problem of ‘what kind of meaning life has in a future with nobody in it’, no one ‘to know, let alone care, that we ever existed’. First I baulked at ‘nobody in it’, because that word ‘nobody’ assumes that only humans have any real presence, any value as survivors; it assumes an anthropocentric viewpoint, which I no longer have, though it is probably true that any remaining forms of life will not care that we ever existed.
articles.title: Lydia Davis · Dying, or Doing Something Else: Marcus Aurelius and Me

articles.blurb: In an age of self-denial, Gary Shteyngart makes the case for martinis, bespoke suits, and expensive watches
articles.description: Skewering a culture obsessed with work, status, and relentless self-improvement, Gary Shteyngart suggests that we indulge in the unexpected wonders of the world.
articles.title: Living His Best Life, and Then Some — The Sensualist: Adventures in Pure Pleasure by Gary Shteyngart

articles.blurb: Robert Frost played the folksy Yankee farmer. His letters reveal grief, guilt, rage, and "a daft tangle of adulterous affairs"
“A problem of our age is that literature — what Barthelme called art — is expected to justify itself; in Barthelme’s time, its value was more self-evident”
articles.title: Too Much Sense, by Lauren Oyler
paragraphs: I was at the Korean restaurant with Kris. The book review walked in, drenched, unspeaking.
“The way to do it would be to read a couple a day starting now. Maybe some days I’d have to do three.”

Weeks later, the book review spoke, dryly: “In the competing methodologies of contemporary criticism, many of them quite rich in implications, a sort of tyranny of great expectations obtains, a rage for final explanations, a refusal to allow a work that mystery which is essential to it.”

Yes, I replied. It’s still true. The biggest problem in Anglophone literature today is that it is boring. It has gotten more boring since Donald Barthelme wrote this line in his 1985 essay “Not-Knowing.” It’s boring for many of the same reasons now as then. Writers and critics express a childish resistance to seeing writing as art, a fear of “not-knowing” that produces immediately legible achievements, or at least competence, organized in normal, immediately legible ways. Writers must avoid surprise, irritation, or confusion; critics even more. Why is this happening? The same reasons we give for all our problems now: internet, AI, capitalism. (In 1985, capitalism was also an issue.) One downstream problem is that, increasingly, people can’t read. This is embarrassing for them—books are still considered cool, somehow, thanks to the same platforms that have distracted us from actually reading them—and distressing to those of us who do it professionally. A result is that literature has become aesthetically conservative. Among the high-minded, modernism, which is a hundred years old, is trendy, albeit best left mimicked by Europeans and the very brave, while postmodernism is treated as an aberrant joke, most often ignored or, in the case of a few canonized male novelists, tolerated. Among the rest of the literary world—publishers, editors, writers—there remains an imperative to make it easier for people to read. The idea is to give them more of what they’re used to, something to which they can’t object, clear prose and recognizable stories. Jane Austen has a proven track record. George Eliot stands the test of time. We should be writing like them! But in simpler language, of course, that a teenager who mainly reads automatically generated captions on TikTok could follow, that leaves no space for misunderstandings, multiple interpretations, or fun.

In May of this year, Picador reissued two short-story anthologies that Barthelme himself compiled while he was alive, Sixty Stories and Forty Stories. The book review is making me state this directly, though I’d prefer to be more oblique, as the subject, an inveterate postmodernist, demands. It’s a little weird that basically no critic or literary journalist seems to have covered these reissues. In the recent past, I don’t think this would have been the case. Many of these stories are beloved by writers and students of writing especially, and he published 129 stories in The New Yorker, plus lots of Comment pieces, before his death in 1989. Because his books are not literally big—most of the stories here are just a few pages long—he has so far avoided the vulgar re[ap]pr[a]isals that have come for many “difficult” male authors of the twentieth century; liking him comes with no social stigma. His difficulty is sort of smoothed over in favor of celebrating the most coherent, and teachable, spots in his oeuvre: the shining stories smudged with just enough oddness to make them easy to love, among them “The Balloon,” “Game,” “Some of Us Had Been Threatening Our Friend Colby,” “The School,” and some of the domestic stories, like “Chablis.” This last is pretty much just a funny, if searching, monologue by an uneasy husband about how his wife wants a dog “for that damn baby.” “What’s that baby going to do with that dog that it can’t do with me?” the narrator wonders. “Romp? I can romp.”

articles.blurb: What happens when humans cease to be the primary agents of intellectual progress? We're about to find out
People love stories of accidental scientific discoveries. But they are mostly, at best, actively misleading
articles.title: Science isn't a series of lucky accidents
articles.description: Let the facts spoil a good dinner party story.
paragraphs: People love accidental discoveries. Penicillin’s discovery by Alexander Fleming is a classic example. Fungal spores wafted in through an open window, fell onto a plate of bacterial colonies, and dissolved them. Another is Louis Pasteur’s discovery of a chicken cholera vaccine, the second vaccine ever developed. After Pasteur left a broth overexposed to oxygen, it went stale. But he ran out of fresh broth, so used it anyway to study the effects of an infection, and found, surprisingly, that it protected the chickens. Or how about the discovery of X-rays? Wilhelm Röntgen was working with a cathode ray tube in a dark room when he suddenly noticed a screen glowing nearby, even though he’d wrapped the tube in cardboard.

Though they’re great stories, I’ve come to believe none of them happened that way. Röntgen had his notes burned after his death, and the story is just a hypothesis. Pasteur was extremely secretive as well, and forbade his family from making his notes and letters public after his death. His grandson, however, did, and after poring over their contents, historians have found that the key experiments were done deliberately by Pasteur’s then-assistant Émile Roux while Pasteur was away for his daughter’s wedding.

And what about Fleming? His first paper describing penicillin in 1929 never says where the spores came from. Of course, it’s hard to see how he could have known, given they would have been microscopic. But Fleming first told the window story in an interview in 1945, sixteen years after his first report, and his colleagues testified the window was ‘seldom if ever opened’. They weren’t able to replicate the discovery as he described, either: penicillin would have needed to be present on the plate before the bacteria grew, because it blocks bacteria from building their cell walls, rather than killing them once they’ve grown.

Several people have tried to work out what really happened. Fleming’s would-be biographer Ronald Hare made dozens of attempts and found just one reliable way to reproduce the discovery that fit the facts. The spores, he argues, were an unusually productive strain; came from the lab of a fungal researcher on the floor below, rather than the window; settled on the plate roughly when Fleming seeded it with bacteria; Fleming forgot to incubate it; and all this happened during a cold spell in the summer that let the mold grow before the bacteria. Hare noted how much more serendipitous this sequence of events was: ‘the odds against the occurrence of the phenomenon become almost astronomical’, though he ultimately believed it. While writing this column, I read through many of his notes and letters archived at the Wellcome Library and have come to agree with his view: Hare was exceedingly careful in corroborating the events from multiple people and sources from the time.

Part of the reason I find the popular stories fascinating is because it’s jarring to realize how little they’re based on. I do expect some stories of accidental discovery will survive the test of time. In medicine, for example, it’s fairly common to test a drug for one disease and find, unexpectedly, that it works for another: colchicine was used for centuries to treat gout before it was found effective against cardiovascular disease, and sildenafil (Viagra) was being tested for angina when its more famous effect was noticed. Side effects are difficult to predict.

articles.blurb: Cruelty, indignity, and the early history of the Americas. A new 700-page work follows North America up to 1680
articles.title: Rethinking the Early History of North America
articles.description: Peter Mancall’s new book reframes the history of the American continent as a zone of encounters between Native peoples, European empires, and African societies.
paragraphs: Another date that has seen a dramatic shift in how it has been memorialized is 1776. Synonymous with the founding of the United States, 1776 has been treated by generations of Americans as part of a broader civilizational story: the westward expansion of European peoples, institutions, and political traditions. Within that framework, national commemorations form essential chapters in a single narrative linking European arrival to nationhood, thus blurring the distinction between the history of Europeans in what would become North America and the history of the United States itself.

But over the past 40 or so years, a remarkable shift has occurred. More recent interpretations attempt to disentangle the history of colonization from that of the US Constitution. In this view, the United States is understood less as the political expression of European settlement than as a particular constitutional project: one grounded in republican government, in the institutions and philosophies articulated in the Declaration and then codified in the Constitution. Such interpretations do not deny the centrality of European colonization to the nation; rather, they critically reexamine North American and US history to foreground the peoples excluded, displaced, or subordinated by it. Native nations, enslaved Africans, and non-Anglo populations claimed as well as rejected the United States. In this interpretive framework, the history of the United States is not reducible to the history of Europeans in North America, even if European settlement formed its precondition.

The 12-hour PBS series The American Revolution reflects this interpretive shift. Its opening episodes foreground historians of Native America, seeking to widen the traditional narrative beyond a familiar story of colonial resistance to Britain. In doing so, the series implicitly asks whether 1776 should be remembered primarily as the triumph of a particular people in its struggle toward self-government, or as the beginning of a contingent experiment in such government. With more than half a dozen historians of Native America foregrounding the latter, the series details how the republic was founded, witnessed, and carried forward by a range of peoples and perspectives—peoples and perspectives that became more diverse with continental expansion.

Into this interpretive fray comes the latest offering in the venerable Oxford History of the United States, a now 10-volume series that, in the words of its publisher, “blends social, political, economic, cultural, diplomatic, and military history into coherent and vividly written narrative.” Initiated under the coeditorship of C. Vann Woodward and Richard Hofstadter in the 1960s, the series has become in many ways the Cadillac of US historical production: tomes written by master craftsmen without a female or minority author among them (yet). The books are not necessarily flashy but instead reflect the boxy and somewhat stodgy assumptions of the postwar historiography from which the series was born: sweeping national narratives organized around the development of the United States as a political, constitutional, and national project.

articles.blurb: Why is the literary establishment turning a blind eye toward likely AI usage in award-winning fiction?
articles.title: The Part About the Machines
articles.description: The news has already traveled the world, but for those who haven’t yet heard: three weeks ago, El País published an article declaring that the award-winning novel Donde el agua trabaja, by Peruvian writer David Silva Rojas, was, according to Pangram, 99 percent AI-generated.
paragraphs: The news has already traveled the world, but for those who haven’t yet heard: three weeks ago, El País published an article declaring that the award-winning novel Donde el agua trabaja, by Peruvian writer David Silva Rojas, was, according to Pangram, 99 percent AI-generated. The program also attributed 97 percent of the author’s answers in a subsequent interview to AI. A personal essay about his writing process: 80 percent AI. And the author’s Instagram post denying his use of artificial intelligence: 84 percent AI.

On November 6th, the Mexican publishing house Almadía reaffirmed its decision to give Silva Rojas the award and publish the book, following what it said was an examination of the “materials provided by the author.” Its statement did not specify which materials, nor did it detail what findings led the publisher to uphold the award.

Silva Rojas’s novel is about a young Peruvian woman who leaves Ayacucho, a southern Andean town, to work the land of a winery in the coastal region of Ica. Since most of the discussion surrounding the novel has been monomaniacally focused on identity, it’s perhaps appropriate to mention that I am a young Peruvian woman, that my entire family is from Ayacucho and Ica, and that many of my relatives—my parents in their youth, my uncles for many years, and my grandparents and great-grandparents for nearly their entire lives—have been agricultural workers. And also that, thanks to the great escalator that is social mobility, I have had one foot in San Francisco for over four years, and have spent much of that time reporting on and following the artificial-intelligence gold rush.1Two additional facts reveal how close this story is to my own life. First: I did my first journalistic internship at El País in mid-2024, although I no longer have any professional ties to the newspaper, nor am I trying to defend it here. Second: like Silva Rojas, I lived in Japan for several years, although I didn’t return writing like Bashō.

As a Peruvian, I can say that Donde el agua trabaja relies on mawkish clichés about the working-class experience in Ica. As a reader, I can say it’s a pretty bad book. And as someone who has spent years in and around the tech world, I can say that, despite Almadía’s statements, it’s hard to believe the novel wasn’t written with the help of artificial intelligence. But as a Latin American writer I’d like to point out something much more concerning. The reaction to these events has been a display of ignorance and obscurantism on the part of many intellectuals from our continent, who have claimed that Pangram “doesn’t work,” who have insisted that the “attack” on Silva is nothing more than a display of racism, and who have, in short, made it clear that what they truly want is to bury their heads in the sand and refuse to confront—beyond the scandal of the new—the arrival of this new technology.

As soon as El País published its report, certain writers proclaimed that AI detectors were also flagging as AI-generated the first page of Frankenstein or the U.S. Constitution. Yet their screenshots came not from Pangram but from TextGuard, a tool that (as an AFP investigation revealed earlier this year) misclassifies human text as AI-generated to then charge its user to “humanize” it. Said differently: those writers spread misinformation based on a fraudulent program. It didn’t matter. Their images went viral, and fueled the popular and erroneous notion that it is impossible to detect AI-written text.2I am not adding the link to these tweets, or to any of the other texts I am criticizing, because my interest here is not to accuse any author, but to show a tragic general trend.

articles.blurb: Patricia Highsmith was rude, bigoted, and indifferent to her readers. Yet few novelists read human character so precisely
articles.title: ‘She was a monster’: the real Patricia Highsmith, by the people who knew her
articles.description: A new film starring Helen Mirren explores the Ripley writer’s later years, but was she really so rude and eccentric? Editors and publishers who worked with her look back
paragraphs: Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes.

“But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”.

Highsmith, who was born in Fort Worth, Texas, in 1921, had a hit with her 1950 debut, Strangers on a Train, boosted by Alfred Hitchcock’s film. A perfect second novel, lesbian road trip The Price of Salt (later republished as Carol), sold a million copies under the pseudonym Claire Morgan, and The Talented Mr Ripley (1955) was a critical success. But around the mid-1960s, Highsmith’s American luck ran out: her agent wrote that her books were “too subtle”, her characters too unlikable, to make it into paperback. By 1984 she was without an American publisher.

“She never found a home because she was so unpleasant,” Penzler says. “I don’t think anybody said, ‘Oh look, we’re losing money but I love her so much, let’s keep her.’” Not yet knowing this, he signed a six-book deal with Highsmith, creating a new imprint in the process. “Pat didn’t want to be identified as a mystery writer, so I started Penzler Books.” He knew Highsmith’s first editor, Joan Kahn. “When I told her I’d bought Pat, she said: ‘God, what’s wrong with you?’ Later we agreed she was a monster.”

In Anton Corbijn’s new film A Talent for Murder, adapted from Joanna Murray-Smith’s 2014 play, Switzerland, a dying Highsmith is played by Helen Mirren, who nails her physicality with dark contact lenses, a wig and a way of seeming to make her neck disappear. By 1995, when the film is set, Highsmith had lived alone for years, ending her last relationship with the translator Monique Buffet, then 27, when she was 66. Tortured by her sexuality, unrequited love and a poisonous mother, happiness largely eluded her.

The film’s premise is that a young American editor must persuade Highsmith to write one last Ripley novel: if she signs, his job is guaranteed and her uncertain legacy assured. It’s a fiction, of course, though lovingly built on real details, from the water glasses filled with cigarettes to her tank of pet snails and the Bond villain bunker she designed.

“A human being is far more valuable than his opinions.” When Gershom Scholem blasted Hannah Arendt, she wondered: could they still be friends?
articles.title: The Knife’s Edge
paragraphs: In October 2016, a colleague phoned Roger Berkowitz, a professor of politics and human rights at Bard College and the founding director of the Hannah Arendt Center, to warn him. A public letter was circulating, accusing Berkowitz of giving a platform to fascism: He had invited a German philosophy professor, by then a member of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), to a conference at Bard. Fifty-six political theorists signed the letter, including the colleague who called. She told him that there was no space in the present moment for views so out of keeping with what the liberal left took to be self-evident. She hoped, however, that they could still be friends. “You have my number,” he told her. “If you disagreed with me, you could have called me before you signed a public letter against me.”

The exchange opens Berkowitz’s new book, A World We Share, which details the political philosopher Hannah Arendt’s sometimes stormy friendships. In it, Berkowitz expresses a vitally important position on friendship, drawing a sharp distinction between his view and that of his colleague. “For her, friendship meant loyalty to a common cause,” he writes, but “for me, it meant loyalty to a shared world.” This slim, elegant book about Arendt’s life among her friends is likewise an attempt to state clearly what her example has to teach us and why it matters more now than it has in a long time.

The usual story is that friendship rests on shared values. We like the people who see the world as we do, and when they stop seeing it that way, something has gone wrong with the friendship. The sorting of American life into tribes has quietly made this model official: Friendship is the private face of agreement, and agreement always comes first. Berkowitz thinks this is exactly backwards, and he has Arendt to prove it.

In 1946, she sent Gershom Scholem her essay “Zionism Reconsidered.” He was furious, accused her of betraying her people, and demanded that she recant. She defended herself but ended her reply not with an argument but with a question: Could they still be friends? She warned him against becoming “a fanatic for truth,” said he had unleashed “an orgy of truth-telling,” and wrote the sentence Berkowitz’s book keeps returning to: “A human being is far more valuable than his opinions.” In 1963, after Arendt published Eichmann in Jerusalem, Scholem charged her with lacking love for the Jewish people. She agreed. “I love in fact only my friends and am fully incapable of any other love.” A people, she said, is an abstraction. One cannot love it. Friendship is loyalty to particular persons, not to positions, and that is why Arendt thought it a sturdier foundation for a shared world than truth, certainty, or being right.

What keeps the book from being one more plea for civility is a phrase Arendt wrote to Kurt Blumenfeld that same year. She had also sent him “Zionism Reconsidered,” knowing he would hate it, and waited five months for a reply that didn’t arrive. “Friendship,” she finally wrote him, “is rare enough, and it is not to be except on the knife’s edge.” Berkowitz takes the phrase for a chapter title, and it is the real center of his argument.

articles.blurb: Editors were once heroic literary figures, spotting and nurturing hidden talent. Conglomeration in publishing has changed all that
articles.title: The End of the Editor
articles.description: On the death of Gary Fisketjon and the rise of Committee Thought
paragraphs: The sudden death of Gary Fisketjon is a major loss for the literary world. He was, certainly, one of the very last of his kind: the superstar literary editor, the lone individual who could be charged with making possible the sort of books that defined a generation and culture. I never met Fisketjon, and only saw him in person once at an event for County Highway, where he was an editor, at a Manhattan bookstore last year. To know Fisketjon, truly, was to read the authors he edited: Cormac McCarthy, Donna Tartt, Bret Easton Ellis, Jay McInerney, and Richard Ford, among many others. He was, by all accounts, an absurdly meticulous editor. Read Ash Carter’s great, exhaustive profile or Matthew Specktor’s wonderful reminiscence of his time working with Fisketjon to get the full sense of the man. When it comes to his legacy, I have little to add to what’s been written already.

What I can do, as a writer working today, is speak on where the editors like Fisketjon have gone. There’s been a tremendous amount of discourse, of late, on contemporary literary publishing, and whether great novels appear anymore. They can and do, but undoubtedly the world that Fisketjon once operated in—high literary fiction from major imprints—is diminished. The books cannot impact the culture in the same way. Often, this is a lament that is made specific to the novel, but it shouldn’t be. Mass culture has fractured and doesn’t exist as it did in the twentieth century. Just as the novel can’t matter as it once did, neither can the new album, hit single, blockbuster film, or even star athlete. There are fewer stars in general, human beings known instantly to tens of millions of people, and those that are, like Taylor Swift or Tom Cruise, came of age in a different era. The stars are legacy stars. The same is true for literary fiction as it is all across the culture. Fame is more a niche concern. Does a writer need to be a star? Maybe not.

And we shouldn’t lament, for that alone, the fading of the Fisketjon era. Gaudy excess, on its own, doesn’t mean anything. I love that Fisketjon held a Richard Ford book party at the Palladium or lived in a sprawling loft with Jay McInerney in downtown Manhattan, but so what? Those are stories, tales, fodder for literary campfires and little more. What does actually did matter about Fisketjon and his contemporaries—legendary editors like the late Sonny Mehta, Gerald Howard, and Gordon Lish, among several others—was the ability they had to follow their own taste and invest in the writers that mattered to them. This is the entire story of Vintage Contemporaries. Fisketjon, a young editor, was handed a small imprint at Random House and permitted to sculpt the list to his liking. He was allowed, with a modest sum of money, to take risks on unknown writers and try to break them out. More importantly, there was nothing terribly unusual about this. Fisketjon, in taste and talent, was a rarity, but not the concept of an editor at a literary imprint being allowed, with some caveats, to decide what authors would appear in print. If Fisketjon, who was in his twenties and thirties during this era, still had to answer to bosses, it was understood that the final call on who got published at his imprint would be his alone.
